one_liner: NumPy's Generator API with PCG64/PCG64DXSM/SFC64 bit generators and ziggurat samplers; about 1.6-2.5x faster than legacy MT19937 RandomState.
what_it_does: numpy.random.Generator (created with np.random.default_rng) draws arrays of samples from dozens of distributions on top of a pluggable BitGenerator: PCG64 (the default), PCG64DXSM, SFC64, Philox or MT19937. It replaces the legacy RandomState/np.random.* functions, which stay frozen on MT19937 for reproducing old results; the method names mostly match, but streams differ, so it is a near drop-in API with different numbers. A C API (bitgen_t plus random_* distribution functions in the static npyrandom library) and ctypes/CFFI/PyCapsule handles let C, Cython and Numba code call the same generators and samplers.
how_it_is_fast: The bit generators are cheaper per 64-bit output than MT19937: PCG64 is a 128-bit LCG with an XSL-RR output permutation, PCG64DXSM uses a cheaper 64-bit multiplier on the LCG step plus a stronger xorshift-multiply (DXSM) output, and SFC64 (from PractRand) is a 256-bit add/xor/shift/rotate generator with no multiplications. Native __uint128_t is used where the compiler has it, with _umul128 emulation on MSVC. Much of the larger gain over RandomState comes from the samplers: ziggurat normals and exponentials instead of Box-Muller and log inversion, and Lemire's nearly divisionless method for bounded integers; draws are made in bulk loops in C with the GIL released.
when_to_use: Python code still calling np.random.* or RandomState for bulk draws: switching to default_rng() gives about 2.2x geometric-mean speedup overall (5.3x for normals, 10.7x for exponentials) on the page's 64-bit Linux run.
Large array draws (the benchmark uses 1,000,000 values per call) of uniforms, ints, normals, exponentials or gammas on 64-bit x86 Linux or Windows.
Raw speed with no jump-ahead needed: SFC64 is the fastest NumPy bit generator (2.5 ns per uint64, 2.6 ns per uniform versus 5.6/5.9 for MT19937), including on 32-bit builds.
Many parallel streams: SeedSequence.spawn or BitGenerator.spawn for independent streams; prefer PCG64DXSM over PCG64 when spawning millions of streams.
C, Cython or Numba code that already ships with NumPy and wants its distribution samplers through the bitgen_t C API instead of writing its own.
when_not_to_use: Plain C++ projects: the measured path is the Python API, and using the C core means linking NumPy's npyrandom and npymath static libraries or copying sources; pcg-cpp or a header-only generator is simpler.
32-bit builds: on 32-bit Windows PCG64 scores 25 and PCG64DXSM 39 versus MT19937 at 100 overall; only SFC64 (77) comes close.
One value at a time in a Python loop: per-call interpreter overhead dominates and the per-value nanosecond figures do not apply.
Laplace, Poisson or binomial-heavy workloads: gains are small or negative (Laplace 76.1 ns with PCG64DXSM versus 73.2 ns with MT19937 under Generator).
Security or cryptography: the docs say these generators are not suitable; use secrets.

integration.form: module (Python package with Cython/C extension); C access via the npyrandom static library shipped in numpy/random/lib
integration.dependencies: Python and NumPy; the C API also needs npymath
integration.min_toolchain: not documented on the pages read; the C sources require C99 or later (pcg64.h errors on nonstandard GNU inline semantics)
integration.platforms: any platform NumPy supports; fast path needs a 64-bit build (native __uint128_t where available, _umul128 emulation on MSVC)
integration.thread_safety: Each BitGenerator carries a shared RLock that Generator methods take while releasing the GIL, so a shared instance is safe but serialized; the docs recommend one Generator per thread via SeedSequence.spawn (multithreading.rst shows 4 threads cutting a 10M-normal fill from 99.6 ms to 32.8 ms).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: Generator mirrors most RandomState method names, but output streams differ and some methods were renamed (for example integers replaces randint), so seeded results are not reproduced

gotchas: Stream compatibility is only promised for the same seed, method calls, NumPy build and machine; Generator algorithms may change in X.Y releases, and default_rng may switch its default bit generator (PCG64DXSM is slated to replace PCG64).

PCG64 (XSL-RR) has a known weakness with millions of randomly seeded streams: two streams sharing the low 58 state bits fail PractRand when interleaved (numpy issue #16313); use PCG64DXSM, SFC64 or Philox at that scale.
SFC64 has no jumped() or advance(); parallel use must go through SeedSequence spawning.
Calling rng.random() five times is not guaranteed to equal rng.random(5); NumPy reserves the right to use different algorithms for different block sizes.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick NumPy's Generator when you are already in the Python/NumPy stack and need many distributions with sound parallel seeding at no integration cost. randomgen (the project this code came from) adds faster bit generators such as Romu and Xoshiro256 with the same interface, and Randompack's paper reports lower per-value times than NumPy (U(0,1) 0.42 versus 1.8 ns); in C++ use pcg-cpp, EigenRand or a SIMD generator instead.
verified_claims_summary: NumPy's own timeit script (min of 3 runs, 1,000,000 values per call) on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X under Ubuntu 20.04 with GCC 9.3.0 gives uniforms in 3.1 ns (PCG64), 2.9 ns (PCG64DXSM) and 2.6 ns (SFC64) versus 5.9 ns for MT19937 under Generator and 6.0 ns for legacy RandomState, for overall geometric-mean speedups over RandomState of 2.19x, 2.25x and 2.51x. Optimization flags are not stated, the baseline is NumPy's own C MT19937 rather than std::mt19937, and 32-bit Windows reverses the result for the PCG generators.
status_note: Actively maintained (32.9k stars, commits on 2026-10-01) and BSD-3-Clause; the Generator API has shipped since NumPy 1.17 and the C sources are small enough to copy if you need the generators without Python.
